system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

You have decided to leave the hospital against medical advice. 
It has been explained to you that you are in alcohol withdrawal, 
which may worsen when you leave. Alcohol withdrawal puts you at 
risk for serious medical complications including seizures and 
death. We believe that you should stay in the hospital for 
monitoring and treatment of your withdrawal. Psychiatry has 
evaluated you and decided that you have the capacity to decide 
to leave against our advice.
. 
You were admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain. An 
ultrasound of your liver and gallbladder was performed, which 
did not show problems with your gallbladder. It is most likely 
that your pain was caused by your gastritis, which was 
exacerbated by alcohol use. You were given medications for 
gastritis and pain. Your pain resolved and you were able to eat 
a regular diet. You should restart your home omeprazole for 
treatment of your gastritis.
.
You experienced symptoms of alcohol withdrawal and received 
medication for this. You wanted to leave the hospital against 
medical advice, and psychiatry was called to evaluate you. They 
determined that you had capacity to decide to leave and gave 
recommendations regarding valium (diazepam) taper. You will be 
discharged to home on valium for your symptoms of withdrawal on 
the following schedule:
.
Day 1 (___): 10 mg valium three times daily (total 30 mg 
this day)
Day 2 (___): 10 mg valium in the morning and evening, 5 mg 
valium in the afternoon (total 25 mg this day) 
Day 3 (___): 10 mg valium twice daily (total 20 mg this 
day)
Day 4 (___): 10 mg valium in the morning, 5 mg valium in 
the evening (total 15 mg this day) 
Day 5 (___): 10 mg valium once (total 10 mg this day) 
Day 6 (___): 5 mg valium once (total 5 mg this day) 
.
Please do not take this medication if you are feeling sleepy or 
confused. Do not drive or operate machinery while taking this 
medication.
.
Please schedule a follow-up appointment with your primary care 
provider for later this week. Please also continue to attend 
your outpatient detoxification program.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

cholecystitis.

COMPARISON:  None.

RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT ULTRASOUND:  Liver is echogenic with enlargement of
caudate lobe and nodular contour .  There is no intrahepatic biliary ductal
dilatation.  Common bile duct measures about 4 mm. Portal vein demonstrates
reversal of flow but appears patent.  There is no gallbladder wall thickening
with no evidence of gallstones or sonographic ___ sign.  The gallbladder
is not significantly distended.  Pancreatic head and neck appear unremarkable.
Pancreatic body and tail are obscured by overlying bowel gas.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Diffuse liver disease with possible cirrhosis. Reversed portal vein flow

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this belly pain for about four days now. It’s up here in the middle, kind of sharp sometimes. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were at another hospital earlier. They thought it might be your gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they did an ultrasound and said maybe gallstones or something in the duct. Gave me antibiotics and sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed that ultrasound. Good news — no gallstones or cholecystitis. But your liver does look abnormal, consistent with cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I already knew I had cirrhosis from drinking. But I’ve been drinking more lately — up to two pints a day the past week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely be making your stomach pain worse. You mentioned gastritis before — this sounds like a flare-up from the alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I was on omeprazole after my last hospital stay. Helped for a while, but I stopped when I started drinking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted you on a similar medication, pantoprazole, to calm the stomach lining. We’ll switch back to your omeprazole when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My belly does feel a bit better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also gave you fluids and pain medicine. Your labs show your liver is struggling — bilirubin is elevated, and your AST is high — but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the alcohol too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The ultrasound also showed reversed blood flow in the portal vein — that’s a sign of portal hypertension, which happens with advanced cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Portal hypertension? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, and it’s why we need to manage your liver health carefully. But right now, we’re focused on your pain and making sure you’re not going into alcohol withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling shaky, anxious. My fingers are tingling. That’s happened before when I stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are classic withdrawal symptoms. We’re monitoring you with a scale called CIWA. Since you’ve had seizures before, we’re giving you IV diazepam to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that — I was in the ICU once before for withdrawal. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything we can to keep you safe. We’ve also given you thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins — important for people with alcohol use history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ve been thinking — I want to try to quit drinking. I’ve got an outpatient detox program, but I keep falling off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We support that. But we’re concerned you’re still in withdrawal. Leaving now could be dangerous — risk of seizures or delirium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I just feel restless here. I think I can manage at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve called psychiatry to evaluate you — they’ll help decide if it’s safe for you to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatrist saw you and believes you understand the risks. They agree you can leave, but recommend a diazepam taper at home to prevent withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take valium — diazepam — on a decreasing schedule over six days. Day one: 10 mg three times. Then gradually less each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I shouldn’t drive or anything while on it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Don’t take it if you’re drowsy or confused. And no driving or heavy machinery. We’re giving you 21 pills — enough for the full taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on all your usual meds — Advair, Suboxone, omeprazole, the rest. Plus a two-day course of thiamine and ongoing multivitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my inhaler more — I’ve got asthma, but it’s been worse lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your Advair and albuterol going. The wheezing is scattered, but your oxygen is good. Just keep using them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stomach — I think I could eat something now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll start you on a regular diet. Your pain has improved, and you’re keeping fluids down — that’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish I hadn’t started drinking again. I know it’s hurting my liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not easy. But you’re taking steps — wanting to detox, coming in for care. That matters. Please follow up with your primary doctor and your outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ll call them tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re being discharged now. We’ve reviewed everything — your pain is better, you’re eating, and you understand the risks of leaving during withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I know it’s against advice, but I feel ready. I’ve got the diazepam plan, my meds, and I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented that you understand the risks — including possible seizures or needing to come back. Please don’t hesitate to return if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. Stay safe, and keep working on your recovery.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with abdominal pain exacerbated by heavy alcohol use. Imaging ruled out gallbladder disease but confirmed cirrhosis and portal hypertension. His pain was attributed to alcoholic gastritis, which improved with proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He exhibited symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, including anxiety and paresthesias, and was treated with IV diazepam. Despite medical advice, he chose to leave the hospital early. Psychiatry confirmed his decisional capacity, and he was discharged on a six-day oral diazepam taper, thiamine, and his usual medications. He demonstrated understanding of the risks and committed to outpatient follow-up.
